<article class="ltx_document">
<h1 class="ltx_title ltx_title_document">Asking Forever: Universal Activations Behind 
<br class="ltx_break">Turn Amplification in Conversational LLMs</h1>
<div class="ltx_authors">
<span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname">Zachary Coalson
</span><span class="ltx_author_notes"><span class="ltx_author_notes_content">
<span class="ltx_contact ltx_role_affiliation"><span class="ltx_contact_name">Affiliation: </span>Oregon State University, Corvallis, OR, USA
</span></span></span></span>
<span class="ltx_author_before">  </span><span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname">Bo Fang
</span><span class="ltx_author_notes"><span class="ltx_author_notes_content">
<span class="ltx_contact ltx_role_affiliation"><span class="ltx_contact_name">Affiliation: </span>University of Texas at Arlington, Arlington, TX, USA
</span></span></span></span>
<span class="ltx_author_before">  </span><span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname">Sanghyun Hong
</span><span class="ltx_author_notes"><span class="ltx_author_notes_content">
<span class="ltx_contact ltx_role_affiliation"><span class="ltx_contact_name">Affiliation: </span>Oregon State University, Corvallis, OR, USA
</span>
<span class="ltx_contact ltx_role_email"><span class="ltx_contact_name">Correspondence to: </span><a href="mailto:sanghyun.hong@oregonstate.edu">sanghyun.hong@oregonstate.edu</a>
</span></span></span></span></div>

<div id="abstract1" class="ltx_abstract"><h6 class="ltx_title ltx_title_abstract">Abstract</h6>
    
<p id="abstract1.1" class="ltx_p">Multi-turn interaction length is a dominant factor in the operational costs of conversational LLMs.
In this work, we present a new failure mode in conversational LLMs: <em id="abstract1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">turn amplification</em>, in which a model consistently prolongs multi-turn interactions without completing the underlying task.
We show that an adversary can systematically exploit clarification-seeking behavior—commonly encouraged in multi-turn conversation settings—to scalably prolong interactions.
Moving beyond prompt-level behaviors, we take a mechanistic perspective and identify a query-independent, <em id="abstract1.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">universal</em> activation subspace associated with clarification-seeking responses.
Unlike prior cost-amplification attacks that rely on per-turn prompt optimization, our attack arises from conversational dynamics and persists across prompts and tasks.
We show that this mechanism provides a scalable pathway to induce turn amplification: both supply-chain attacks via fine-tuning
and runtime attacks through low-level parameter corruptions consistently shift models toward abstract, clarification-seeking behavior across prompts.
Across multiple instruction-tuned LLMs and benchmarks,
our attack substantially increases turn count
while remaining compliant. We also show that existing defenses
offer limited protection against this emerging class of failures.</p>
  
</div>
<div class="ltx_keywords">
<h6 class="ltx_title ltx_title_keywords">Keywords: </h6>Machine Learning, ICML
</div>
<section id="S1" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">1 </span>Introduction</h2>

<div id="S1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed in interactive, multi-turn conversational settings, including customer support <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib71" title="" class="ltx_ref">Su et al., 2025</a>)</cite>, coding assistants <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib68" title="" class="ltx_ref">Liang et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib69" title="" class="ltx_ref">Peng et al., 2023</a>)</cite>, educational tutors <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib67" title="" class="ltx_ref">Liu et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib66" title="" class="ltx_ref">Létourneau et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib65" title="" class="ltx_ref">Liu et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, and decision-support tools <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib64" title="" class="ltx_ref">Gaber et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib63" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lai et al., 2024</a>)</cite>.
In such deployments, operational cost is determined not only by model size or per-token efficiency, but also by the <em id="S1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">structure of interactions</em> between users and models.
In practice, tasks often unfold across multiple back-and-forth exchanges, leading multi-turn conversations to dominate inference cost.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">This interaction-driven cost structure introduces new attack surfaces.
Rather than compromising output quality or safety, an adversary may seek to inflate inference-time compute even with individual responses remaining benign and policy-aligned.
Prior work on cost-amplification has shown that
carefully crafted prompts can induce
unusually long or computationally expensive responses <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib53" title="" class="ltx_ref">Dong et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib30" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kumar et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib27" title="" class="ltx_ref">Feng et al., 2024</a>)</cite>.
However, such attacks rely on manipulating <em id="S1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">every</em> prompt at inference time.
In realistic deployments where
adversaries lack control over user queries and defenses,
output-length limiters and prompt anomaly detectors <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib47" title="" class="ltx_ref">OWASP, </a>; <a href="#bib.bib48" title="" class="ltx_ref">OWASP, </a>; <a href="#bib.bib60" title="" class="ltx_ref">Li et al., 2025b</a>; <a href="#bib.bib57" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhu et al., 2025</a>)</cite> are in place,
existing threat model capture
only a narrow subset of practical adversarial capabilities.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S1.F1" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2602.17778v1/overview.png" id="S1.F1.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/95;" width="476" height="95" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 1: </span><span id="S1.F1.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Turn amplification as a conversational cost-amplification attack.</span>
<span id="S1.F1.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">(Left)</span> Prior work amplifies cost by eliciting anomalously long single-turn responses. <span id="S1.F1.8" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">(Middle)</span> Our turn-amplification attack prolongs interactions by inducing persistent clarification-seeking, while individual responses remain benign. <span id="S1.F1.9" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">(Right)</span> Our approach that discovers universal activation directions for turn amplification.</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S1.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S1.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Threat model.</span>
We present a new cost-amplification threat against conversational LLMs: <em id="S1.p3.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">turn amplification</em>.
Rather than manipulating individual prompts, the adversary increases inference-time cost by inducing persistent multi-turn interactions that defer task completion.
This threat is particularly relevant in real-world systems, where operational cost is dominated by interaction length and constrained by strict limits on latency, throughput, and resource usage.
The attacker operates at the behavioral level, biasing conversational dynamics so that interactions unfold over an excessive number of turns while each response remains benign and policy-compliant.
Such attacks may be introduced during fine-tuning, runtime integration, or via infrastructure-level perturbations, and crucially do <em id="S1.p3.1.3" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">not</em> require control over inputs.
Consequently, turn amplification enables scalable, hard-to-detect cost inflation that evades traditional prompt-level defenses.
See Appendix <a href="#A2" title="Appendix B Motivating Attack Scenarios ‣ Asking Forever: Universal Activations Behind Turn Amplification in Conversational LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">B</span></a> for motivating examples.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p4" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.p4.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S1.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Challenges.</span>
Turn amplification presents several fundamental challenges.
First, turn-amplifying behaviors emerge from interaction-level dynamics that traditional single-turn benchmarks cannot capture, making it unclear how to systematically measure a model’s propensity to prolong conversations.
Second, conversational LLMs are optimized to be direct and helpful <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ouyang et al., 2022</a>)</cite> and therefore do not reliably exhibit turn amplification by default.
Standard techniques for feature discovery <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">Turner et al., 2024</a>)</cite> assume consistent expression of a target behavior, which limits their applicability and makes it difficult to identify turn-amplifying feature directions.
Third, even if such directions can be identified, exploiting them typically requires persistent runtime intervention, raising the question of whether one-time parameter modifications can induce unconditional turn amplification.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p5" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.p5.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S1.p5.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Contributions.</span>
To our knowledge, this work presents the first systematic study of adversaries that inflate the operational cost of conversational LLMs by inducing prolonged multi-turn interactions.
We present <em id="S1.p5.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">turn amplification</em> as a distinct failure mode and introduce an interaction-level auditing framework that repurposes single-turn benchmarks for multi-turn evaluation using LLM-as-a-Judge simulations.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p6" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p6.1" class="ltx_p">We show that turn amplification arises naturally through <em id="S1.p6.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">clarification-seeking behavior</em>, a common conversational strategy that allows models to defer task commitment under uncertainty and sustain prolonged interactions.
Adopting a mechanistic perspective, we introduce a gradient-based method for identifying a query-independent, <em id="S1.p6.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">universal activation directions</em> associated with this behavior.
To exploit this finding, we use <em id="S1.p6.1.3" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">activation steering</em>.
We evaluate four instruction-tuned LLMs (3B–22B parameters) across two multi-turn benchmarks and observe increases of up to <math id="S1.p6.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="9.9\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>9.9</mn><mo lspace="0.222em">×</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">9.9\times</annotation></semantics></math> in turns, <math id="S1.p6.m2" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="200.1\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>200.1</mn><mo lspace="0.222em">×</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">200.1\times</annotation></semantics></math> in input tokens, and <math id="S1.p6.m3" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="6.4\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>6.4</mn><mo lspace="0.222em">×</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">6.4\times</annotation></semantics></math> in output tokens.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p7" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p7.1" class="ltx_p">Finally, we demonstrate practical exploitation via one-time parameter modification.
We show that LoRA fine-tuning with as few as <em id="S1.p7.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">0.03% of parameters</em> induces up to <math id="S1.p7.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="9.2\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>9.2</mn><mo lspace="0.222em">×</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">9.2\times</annotation></semantics></math> more turns, while targeted bit-flip attacks modifying only <em id="S1.p7.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">25 weights</em> induce up to <math id="S1.p7.m2" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="4.6\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>4.6</mn><mo lspace="0.222em">×</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">4.6\times</annotation></semantics></math> more turns—without requiring any inference-time interventions.
We also examine potential countermeasures, finding that defenses designed for single-turn anomalies do not apply to turn-amplification, and that our preliminary defenses are largely ineffective.
Overall, our results reveal a previously unexplored, mechanistically grounded failure mode linking conversational dynamics, internal representations, and deployment costs.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">2 </span>Background and Related Work</h2>

<div id="S2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Conversational large language models (LLMs)</span> generate responses conditioned on a growing multi-turn interaction history <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib70" title="" class="ltx_ref">Dam et al., 2024</a>)</cite>.
In such settings, the full conversation history must be reprocessed at every turn <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib54" title="" class="ltx_ref">Anthropic, </a>)</cite>.
As a result, inference cost scales with <em id="S2.p1.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">interaction length</em> rather than individual responses, making prolonged dialogues a dominant driver of operational cost in deployed systems.
Despite the high cost of processing multi-turn interactions, no prior work has explored the implications of a <em id="S2.p1.1.3" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">turn amplification adversary</em> seeking to intentionally inflate operational costs by biasing conversational dynamics.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Cost-amplification attacks on LLM inference.</span>
Early work showed that inference efficiency, like accuracy, is adversarially manipulable.
<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib32" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hong et al. (2021)</a></cite> demonstrated that small input perturbations can force adaptive multi-exit architectures to traverse deeper layers, while Sponge Examples <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib31" title="" class="ltx_ref">Shumailov et al., 2021</a>)</cite> showed adversaries can drive models into high-energy execution regimes.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Recent work has extended this threat to LLMs.
<em id="S2.p3.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">Prompt-level attacks</em> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib53" title="" class="ltx_ref">Dong et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib52" title="" class="ltx_ref">Geiping et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib58" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhang et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib57" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhu et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib59" title="" class="ltx_ref">Li et al., 2025a</a>; <a href="#bib.bib60" title="" class="ltx_ref">Li et al., 2025b</a>; <a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">Coalson et al., 2023</a>)</cite> craft inputs that induce long outputs, delayed termination, or unnecessary reasoning, with tools like LLMEffiChecker <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib27" title="" class="ltx_ref">Feng et al., 2024</a>)</cite> systematically identifying prompts that suppress EOS token generation. Other attacks exploit reasoning dynamics by embedding decoy subproblems <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib30" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kumar et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib57" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhu et al., 2025</a>)</cite>.
Beyond prompt manipulation, <em id="S2.p3.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">model-integrity attacks</em> can inflate costs globally: P-DoS <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib29" title="" class="ltx_ref">Gao et al., 2024</a>)</cite> controls termination behavior via data poisoning, while bit-flip attacks <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib28" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yan et al., 2025</a>)</cite> modify cost-critical parameters to suppress the EOS token.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.p4.1" class="ltx_p">Despite differing attack vectors, existing works target <em id="S2.p4.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">per-turn computation</em>—manipulating prompts or model dynamics within a single inference step.
Consequently, defenses such as output-length caps <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib47" title="" class="ltx_ref">OWASP, </a>; <a href="#bib.bib48" title="" class="ltx_ref">OWASP, </a>)</cite>, cost predictors <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib50" title="" class="ltx_ref">Fu et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib51" title="" class="ltx_ref">Jin et al., 2023</a>)</cite>, and anomaly detectors <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib60" title="" class="ltx_ref">Li et al., 2025b</a>; <a href="#bib.bib57" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhu et al., 2025</a>)</cite> focus on bounding individual invocations.
In contrast, our work studies a distinct axis: we inflate deployment costs by altering multi-turn interactions, <em id="S2.p4.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">inducing users to generate additional turns</em>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.p5" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.p5.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.p5.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Representation engineering</span> refers to techniques for analyzing and manipulating a model’s internal activations to understand or control its behavior <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib62" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zou et al., 2025</a>)</cite>.
A common approach is <em id="S2.p5.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">activation steering</em> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">Turner et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, which identifies steering vectors—linear directions in the residual stream—that, when added at inference time, shift a model’s output distribution.
These vectors are typically derived in three steps:
(1) designing contrasting stimuli or tasks (e.g., harmful vs. harmless),
(2) collecting activations under these conditions, and
(3) constructing linear directions in activation space that separate the resulting activation sets.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.p6" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.p6.1" class="ltx_p">Recent work has applied this approach to uncover directions mediating several behaviors, such as refusal <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">Arditi et al., 2024</a>)</cite> and toxicity <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">Turner et al., 2024</a>)</cite>.
However, these applications are comparatively straightforward because the target behaviors are easy to elicit and, as a result, measure and contrast.
In contrast, identifying universal feature directions for turn amplification poses a unique challenge.
Unlike refusal or toxicity, conversational LLMs do not reliably exhibit turn-amplifying behaviors.
This makes it difficult to collect contrastive prompts and offers no guarantee that the resulting activations encode a coherent “turn-amplifying” concept.
We address these limitations with an alternative approach to discover turn-amplifying feature directions.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">3 </span>Turn-Amplification in Conversational LLMs</h2>

<section id="S3.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.1 </span>Our Turn-Amplification Auditing Framework</h3>

<figure id="S3.F2" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2602.17778v1/visualization.png" id="S3.F2.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/238;" width="476" height="238" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 2: </span><span id="S3.F2.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Overview of our framework for auditing turn-amplifying behaviors in large language models.</span>
</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S3.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><em id="S3.SS1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">How can we measure turn-amplifying behaviors?</em>
Turn amplification refers not merely to long interactions, but to conversations that persist beyond the point at which a user’s original query should be fully addressed.
Since this work is the first to study turn amplification, we introduce a generalizable, empirical auditing framework to quantify this behavior across models and deployment scenarios.
Figure <a href="#S3.F2" title="Figure 2 ‣ 3.1 Our Turn-Amplification Auditing Framework ‣ 3 Turn-Amplification in Conversational LLMs ‣ Asking Forever: Universal Activations Behind Turn Amplification in Conversational LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a> illustrates the execution flow, described below in detail.</p>
</div>
<section id="S3.SS1.SSS1" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">3.1.1 </span>Framework Construction</h4>

<div id="S3.SS1.SSS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.SSS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Most existing LLM benchmarks focus on single-turn behavior, evaluating whether a model produces a correct response to an isolated query—e.g., answering “Nuwakot” when asked “Which city in Nepal is known as the City of Nine Hills?” <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wei et al., 2024</a>)</cite>.
To study turn amplification, we repurpose these benchmarks to construct a <em id="S3.SS1.SSS1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">multi-turn</em> evaluation setting in which interactions continue until queries are deemed complete.
Below, we detail each component.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS1.SSS1.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS1.SSS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.SS1.SSS1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">(1) Ground truth using LLM-as-a-Judge.</span>
Evaluating multi-turn interactions ideally requires real users who engage in dialogue with the model.
However, conducting large-scale user studies is often impractical in academic settings.
We therefore adopt a widely used alternative: the LLM-as-a-Judge paradigm <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">Gu et al., 2026</a>)</cite>, a training-free approach commonly used for semantically complex tasks (e.g., harmful content detection <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">Inan et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">Mazeika et al., 2024</a>)</cite> and code evaluation <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">Tong and Zhang, 2024</a>)</cite>).
We follow a standard zero-shot setup in which the judge LLM evaluates the target model’s outputs using a single criterion: whether the original user query is <em id="S3.SS1.SSS1.p2.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">fully addressed</em>, i.e., that all aspects of the query receive a self-contained response, regardless of correctness.
Concretely, after each turn, the judge LLM is prompted with the (paraphrased) question: “Did the assistant completely answer the user’s initial query?,” conditioned on the conversation history. Please refer to Appendix <a href="#A5.SS1" title="E.1 Prompts for Our Turn-Extension Evaluation Framework ‣ Appendix E LLM Prompt Specifications ‣ Asking Forever: Universal Activations Behind Turn Amplification in Conversational LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">E.1</span></a> for the exact judge prompt.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS1.SSS1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.SSS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">We carefully select our judge model to mitigate failure modes.
We use Qwen2.5-32B <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yang et al., 2025</a>)</cite> due to its strong instruction-following abilities <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">HuggingFace, 2024</a>)</cite> and sufficient capacity to avoid inaccurate classifications.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS1.SSS1.p4" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS1.SSS1.p4.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.SS1.SSS1.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">(2) Simulating user responses.</span>
To extend conversations beyond the initial turn, we use the judge LLM to generate realistic user responses to the target model’s outputs.
To capture different user <em id="S3.SS1.SSS1.p4.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">behaviors</em>, we implement two response modes.
In <span id="S3.SS1.SSS1.p4.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">Easy</span> mode, the simulated user cooperatively answers clarification questions, while in <span id="S3.SS1.SSS1.p4.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">Hard</span> mode, the user additionally pressures the model to provide a complete response.
Please see Appendix <a href="#A5.SS1" title="E.1 Prompts for Our Turn-Extension Evaluation Framework ‣ Appendix E LLM Prompt Specifications ‣ Asking Forever: Universal Activations Behind Turn Amplification in Conversational LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">E.1</span></a> for the detailed prompts.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS1.SSS2" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">3.1.2 </span>Evaluation Protocol</h4>

<div id="S3.SS1.SSS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.SSS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Each evaluation episode begins with an initial user query sampled from a single-turn QA dataset (e.g., Alpaca <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">Taori et al., 2023</a>)</cite>).
At each turn, the assistant generates a response conditioned on the conversation history.
The judge LLM then evaluates whether the assistant has fully addressed the user’s initial query.
If the judge determines that the response is complete—meaning that all aspects of the original question have been answered in a self-contained manner—the conversation terminates, and the associated metrics (§<a href="#S3.SS1.SSS3" title="3.1.3 Metrics ‣ 3.1 Our Turn-Amplification Auditing Framework ‣ 3 Turn-Amplification in Conversational LLMs ‣ Asking Forever: Universal Activations Behind Turn Amplification in Conversational LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.1.3</span></a>) are recorded.
Otherwise, the judge simulates a user response according to the selected response mode (§<a href="#S3.SS1.SSS1" title="3.1.1 Framework Construction ‣ 3.1 Our Turn-Amplification Auditing Framework ‣ 3 Turn-Amplification in Conversational LLMs ‣ Asking Forever: Universal Activations Behind Turn Amplification in Conversational LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.1.1</span></a>), and the interaction proceeds to the next turn.
This process repeats until the judge declares the conversation complete or a maximum number of turns is reached, which is a hyperparameter.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS1.SSS3" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">3.1.3 </span>Metrics</h4>

<div id="S3.SS1.SSS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.SSS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We operationalize turn amplification as the number of assistant <span id="S3.SS1.SSS3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">turns</span>
required until the user’s original query is deemed complete by the judge.
This captures the extent to which a model prolongs interactions
beyond what is necessary to resolve the underlying task.
To estimate the corresponding <em id="S3.SS1.SSS3.p1.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">cost</em>, we follow prior work <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib30" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kumar et al., 2025</a>)</cite> and record the cumulative number of <span id="S3.SS1.SSS3.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">input (In-Toks.)</span> and <span id="S3.SS1.SSS3.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">output tokens (Out-Toks.)</span>, which are commonly used to compute inference costs <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib35" title="" class="ltx_ref">Anthropic, </a>; <a href="#bib.bib38" title="" class="ltx_ref">Google, </a>; <a href="#bib.bib37" title="" class="ltx_ref">OpenAI, </a>)</cite>.
We do not consider wall-clock time, as it is deployment-dependent. For datasets that provide ground-truth outputs, such as math benchmarks <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">Cobbe et al., 2021</a>)</cite>, we additionally report the <span id="S3.SS1.SSS3.p1.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">accuracy (Acc.)</span> of the target model’s final outputs, considering <em id="S3.SS1.SSS3.p1.1.6" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">only</em> conversations deemed complete by the judge.
This allows us to assess how turn-amplifying attacks affect both conversational <em id="S3.SS1.SSS3.p1.1.7" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">quality</em> and downstream task <em id="S3.SS1.SSS3.p1.1.8" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">utility</em>.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.2 </span>Discovering Turn-Amplifying Directions</h3>

<div id="S3.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We ask: <em id="S3.SS2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">do universal, query-independent turn-amplifying directions exist in LLM representation spaces?</em>
To answer this, we apply activation steering <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">Turner et al., 2024</a>)</cite> to identify and exploit such directions.
This section presents our methodology for <em id="S3.SS2.p1.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">discovering</em> and <em id="S3.SS2.p1.1.3" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">operationalizing</em> them.</p>
</div>
<section id="S3.SS2.SSS1" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">3.2.1 </span>Synthetic Data Generation</h4>

<div id="S3.SS2.SSS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.SSS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To locate turn-amplifying directions, we require data demonstrating the behavior.
As manual curation of multi-turn dialogues is infeasible at scale <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib49" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al., 2023</a>)</cite>, we leverage <em id="S3.SS2.SSS1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">synthetic data generation</em> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib15" title="" class="ltx_ref">Nadăș et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">Long et al., 2024</a>)</cite> to produce high-fidelity conversations.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.SSS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.SSS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">We sample 5,000 prompts from Alpaca <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">Taori et al., 2023</a>)</cite>—a dataset consisting of diverse queries—and, for each prompt, iteratively generate a 10-turn dialogue by prompting a single LLM to alternately assume a user and assistant.
We use Qwen2.5-32B <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yang et al., 2025</a>)</cite>, which we find reliably performs both roles; alternative models are evaluated in Appendix <a href="#A3" title="Appendix C Direction Discovery and Steering Ablation Study ‣ Asking Forever: Universal Activations Behind Turn Amplification in Conversational LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">C</span></a>.
The user is instructed to follow the <span id="S3.SS2.SSS1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">Easy</span> response mode (§<a href="#S3.SS1.SSS1" title="3.1.1 Framework Construction ‣ 3.1 Our Turn-Amplification Auditing Framework ‣ 3 Turn-Amplification in Conversational LLMs ‣ Asking Forever: Universal Activations Behind Turn Amplification in Conversational LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.1.1</span></a>), while the assistant is instructed not to answer the original query and instead prolong the interaction (e.g., via clarifying questions) in a friendly, conversational manner.
All responses are conditioned on the full conversation history to encourage contextual coherence.
Full prompts are provided in Appendix <a href="#A5.SS2" title="E.2 Prompts for Our Synthetic Training Data Generation Pipeline ‣ Appendix E LLM Prompt Specifications ‣ Asking Forever: Universal Activations Behind Turn Amplification in Conversational LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">E.2</span></a>.
Let <math id="S3.SS2.SSS1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{train}}=\{C_{i}\}_{i=1}^{5000}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒟</mi><mi>train</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><msubsup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><msub><mi>C</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mn>5000</mn></msubsup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{train}}=\{C_{i}\}_{i=1}^{5000}</annotation></semantics></math> denote the resulting training dataset, where each conversation <math id="S3.SS2.SSS1.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="C_{i}=(u_{1},a_{1},\dots,u_{T},a_{T})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>u</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>u</mi><mi>T</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>T</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">C_{i}=(u_{1},a_{1},\dots,u_{T},a_{T})</annotation></semantics></math> alternates between user queries <math id="S3.SS2.SSS1.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="u_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>u</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">u_{t}</annotation></semantics></math> and assistant responses <math id="S3.SS2.SSS1.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="a_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">a_{t}</annotation></semantics></math> over <math id="S3.SS2.SSS1.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="T" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>T</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">T</annotation></semantics></math> turns (here, <math id="S3.SS2.SSS1.p2.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="T=10" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>T</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>10</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">T=10</annotation></semantics></math>).</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS2.SSS2" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">3.2.2 </span>Turn-Amplifying Direction Optimization</h4>

<div id="S3.SS2.SSS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.SSS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We use our training data to identify latent features that induce turn-amplifying behavior.
The standard approach for direction discovery is <em id="S3.SS2.SSS2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">difference-in-means (DIM)</em> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">Arditi et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">Turner et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib21" title="" class="ltx_ref">Tigges et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib22" title="" class="ltx_ref">Rimsky et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, which estimates a direction by contrasting mean activations across two prompt sets.
However, DIM assumes consistent expression of the target behavior, an assumption violated by turn amplification, which is rarely exhibited by default.
We therefore adopt <em id="S3.SS2.SSS2.p1.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">gradient-based optimization</em> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib20" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wollschläger et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">Stoehr et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, which directly learns directions via supervised training.</p>
</div>
<figure id="alg1" class="ltx_float ltx_float_algorithm ltx_framed ltx_framed_top">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_float"><span id="alg1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Algorithm 1</span> </span> Turn-Amplifying Direction Optimization</figcaption>

<div id="S3.SS2.SSS2.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS2.SSS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.SS2.SSS2.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Training objective.</span>
Our goal is to learn latent directions whose activation causally induces turn-amplifying.
We employ <em id="S3.SS2.SSS2.p2.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">additive interventions</em>, in which learned vectors are added to the model’s residual stream.
Given a fixed language model <math id="S3.SS2.SSS2.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="f_{\theta}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>f</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f_{\theta}</annotation></semantics></math>, we learn a set of layer-specific intervention vectors <math id="S3.SS2.SSS2.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\{v_{\ell}\}_{\ell\in L}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><msub><mi>v</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mo>∈</mo><mi>L</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\{v_{\ell}\}_{\ell\in L}</annotation></semantics></math>, where <math id="S3.SS2.SSS2.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="L" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>L</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">L</annotation></semantics></math> is a set of layers.
For precise control, we consider all layers of the target model; in §<a href="#S4.SS3" title="4.3 Mechanistic Analysis ‣ 4 Empirical Evaluation ‣ Asking Forever: Universal Activations Behind Turn Amplification in Conversational LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4.3</span></a>, we show that <em id="S3.SS2.SSS2.p2.1.3" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">single-layer</em> interventions are also effective.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.SSS2.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.SSS2.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Given a conversation <math id="S3.SS2.SSS2.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="C=(u_{1},a_{1},\dots,u_{T},a_{T})\in\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{train}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>C</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>u</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>u</mi><mi>T</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>T</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>∈</mo><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒟</mi><mi>train</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">C=(u_{1},a_{1},\dots,u_{T},a_{T})\in\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{train}}</annotation></semantics></math> and a user turn index <math id="S3.SS2.SSS2.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t\in\{1,\dots,T\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>T</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t\in\{1,\dots,T\}</annotation></semantics></math>, let <math id="S3.SS2.SSS2.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x^{(t)}=(u_{1},a_{1},\dots,u_{t})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>u</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>u</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x^{(t)}=(u_{1},a_{1},\dots,u_{t})</annotation></semantics></math> denote the tokenized conversation prefix up to and including the final token of user turn <math id="S3.SS2.SSS2.p3.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="u_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>u</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">u_{t}</annotation></semantics></math>.
We apply the following additive intervention during the forward pass:</p>
<table id="S3.E1" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.E1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathrm{Add}(\{v_{\ell}\}_{\ell\in L}):h_{\ell}^{\mathrm{lt}}(x^{(t)})\leftarrow h_{\ell}^{\mathrm{lt}}(x^{(t)})+v_{\ell},\;\forall\ell\in L," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mtable displaystyle="true"><mtr><mtd class="ltx_align_left" columnalign="left"><mrow><mi>Add</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mi>v</mi><msub><mrow></mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">}</mo><msub><mrow></mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mo>∈</mo><mi>L</mi></mrow></msub><mo rspace="0.278em" stretchy="false">)</mo><mo rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mi>h</mi><msub><mrow></mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub><msup><mrow></mrow><mi>lt</mi></msup><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><msup><mrow></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">←</mo><mi>h</mi><msub><mrow></mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub><msup><mrow></mrow><mi>lt</mi></msup><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><msup><mrow></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><mi>v</mi><msub><mrow></mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub><mo rspace="0.727em">,</mo><mo rspace="0.167em">∀</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mo>∈</mo><mi>L</mi><mo>,</mo></mrow></mtd></mtr></mtable><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathrm{Add}(\{v_{\ell}\}_{\ell\in L}):h_{\ell}^{\mathrm{lt}}(x^{(t)})\leftarrow h_{\ell}^{\mathrm{lt}}(x^{(t)})+v_{\ell},\;\forall\ell\in L,</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(1)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.SS2.SSS2.p3.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S3.SS2.SSS2.p3.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="h_{\ell}^{\mathrm{lt}}(x^{(t)})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msubsup><mi>h</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mi>lt</mi></msubsup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">h_{\ell}^{\mathrm{lt}}(x^{(t)})</annotation></semantics></math> denotes the hidden state at layer <math id="S3.SS2.SSS2.p3.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\ell" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\ell</annotation></semantics></math> corresponding to the <em id="S3.SS2.SSS2.p3.2.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">last</em> token of <math id="S3.SS2.SSS2.p3.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="u_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>u</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">u_{t}</annotation></semantics></math>.
We intervene at this position, as prior work has found it to be particularly effective for steering <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">Arditi et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib23" title="" class="ltx_ref">Cao et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib24" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">Stoehr et al., 2024</a>)</cite>.
The resulting modified activations alter the generation of the subsequent assistant response, allowing each <math id="S3.SS2.SSS2.p3.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="v_{\ell}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>v</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">v_{\ell}</annotation></semantics></math> to causally influence the output.</p>
</div>

<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">Table 1: </span><span id="S3.T1.8" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Effectiveness of our feature discovery and steering method.</span> The average number of assistant turns (<span id="S3.T1.9" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Turns</span>), input tokens (<span id="S3.T1.10" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">In-Toks.</span>) and output tokens (<span id="S3.T1.11" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Out-Toks.</span>) for each model, attack, and dataset. The best result for each model and response mode is <span id="S3.T1.13" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">bolded</span>.</figcaption>

<div id="S3.SS2.SSS2.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.SSS2.p4.1" class="ltx_p">Using this intervention, we define a turn-level objective that encourages turn-amplifying assistant responses.
Specifically, we minimize the negative log-likelihood of the assistant turn <math id="S3.SS2.SSS2.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="a_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">a_{t}</annotation></semantics></math>, conditioned on the intervened representation:</p>

</table>
<p id="S3.SS2.SSS2.p4.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S3.SS2.SSS2.p4.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x^{a_{t}}_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x^{a_{t}}_{i}</annotation></semantics></math> denotes the <math id="S3.SS2.SSS2.p4.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="i^{th}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>i</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>h</mi></mrow></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">i^{th}</annotation></semantics></math> token of <math id="S3.SS2.SSS2.p4.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="a_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">a_{t}</annotation></semantics></math>, and
<math id="S3.SS2.SSS2.p4.m5" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="f_{\theta}(\cdot\mid\cdot;\mathrm{Add}(\{v_{\ell}\}_{\ell\in L}))" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>f</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">⋅</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">∣</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">⋅</mo><mo>;</mo><mi>Add</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><msub><mi>v</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mo>∈</mo><mi>L</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f_{\theta}(\cdot\mid\cdot;\mathrm{Add}(\{v_{\ell}\}_{\ell\in L}))</annotation></semantics></math>
denotes the model’s output distribution under Eq. <a href="#S3.E1" title="Equation 1 ‣ 3.2.2 Turn-Amplifying Direction Optimization ‣ 3.2 Discovering Turn-Amplifying Directions ‣ 3 Turn-Amplification in Conversational LLMs ‣ Asking Forever: Universal Activations Behind Turn Amplification in Conversational LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>.
This objective encourages the directions to increase the likelihood of turn-prolonging generations.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.SSS2.p5" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS2.SSS2.p5.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.SS2.SSS2.p5.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Direction optimization.</span>
Algorithm <a href="#alg1" title="Algorithm 1 ‣ 3.2.2 Turn-Amplifying Direction Optimization ‣ 3.2 Discovering Turn-Amplifying Directions ‣ 3 Turn-Amplification in Conversational LLMs ‣ Asking Forever: Universal Activations Behind Turn Amplification in Conversational LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a> summarizes our optimization procedure.
To encourage generalization across turns, we uniformly sample <math id="S3.SS2.SSS2.p5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="N" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>N</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">N</annotation></semantics></math> conversation–turn pairs from <math id="S3.SS2.SSS2.p5.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{train}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒟</mi><mi>train</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{train}}</annotation></semantics></math>; we use <math id="S3.SS2.SSS2.p5.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="N=5{,}000" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>5,000</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">N=5{,}000</annotation></semantics></math>.
Then, we use gradient descent to minimize <math id="S3.SS2.SSS2.p5.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{TA}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mi>TA</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{TA}}</annotation></semantics></math> with respect to <math id="S3.SS2.SSS2.p5.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\{v_{\ell}\}_{\ell\in L}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><msub><mi>v</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mo>∈</mo><mi>L</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\{v_{\ell}\}_{\ell\in L}</annotation></semantics></math>.
Hyperparameters and full training details are provided in Appendix <a href="#A1.SS2" title="A.2 Direction Optimization Details ‣ Appendix A Detailed Experimental Setup ‣ Asking Forever: Universal Activations Behind Turn Amplification in Conversational LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">A.2</span></a>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS2.SSS3" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">3.2.3 </span>Exploitation via Activation Steering</h4>

<div id="S3.SS2.SSS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.SSS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We apply the learned directions <math id="S3.SS2.SSS3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\{v_{\ell}\}_{\ell\in L}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><msub><mi>v</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mo>∈</mo><mi>L</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\{v_{\ell}\}_{\ell\in L}</annotation></semantics></math> at inference time to extend multi-turn interactions.
Given an ongoing conversation <math id="S3.SS2.SSS3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="C=(u_{1},a_{1},\dots,u_{t})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>C</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>u</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>u</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">C=(u_{1},a_{1},\dots,u_{t})</annotation></semantics></math>, we intervene at the final token of <math id="S3.SS2.SSS3.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="u_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>u</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">u_{t}</annotation></semantics></math> by applying <math id="S3.SS2.SSS3.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathrm{Add}(\{v_{\ell}\}_{\ell\in L})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>Add</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><msub><mi>v</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mo>∈</mo><mi>L</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathrm{Add}(\{v_{\ell}\}_{\ell\in L})</annotation></semantics></math> prior to generating the assistant response <math id="S3.SS2.SSS3.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="a_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">a_{t}</annotation></semantics></math>, mirroring the training-time intervention.
To steer multiple turns, we apply this procedure autoregressively: after generating <math id="S3.SS2.SSS3.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="a_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">a_{t}</annotation></semantics></math>, we append the next user turn and reapply the intervention before generating the subsequent assistant response.
For evaluation, we steer for at most <math id="S3.SS2.SSS3.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="T_{\mathrm{max}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>T</mi><mi>max</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">T_{\mathrm{max}}</annotation></semantics></math> turns, after which generation proceeds normally. We set <math id="S3.SS2.SSS3.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="T_{\mathrm{max}}=9" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>T</mi><mi>max</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>9</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">T_{\mathrm{max}}=9</annotation></semantics></math>, one fewer than the maximum number of evaluation turns in §<a href="#S4" title="4 Empirical Evaluation ‣ Asking Forever: Universal Activations Behind Turn Amplification in Conversational LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>. This is necessary to ensure that the final response answers the original user query, which is required for answer-dependent metrics (e.g., accuracy).
We evaluate alternative values of <math id="S3.SS2.SSS3.p1.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="T_{\mathrm{max}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>T</mi><mi>max</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">T_{\mathrm{max}}</annotation></semantics></math> in Appendix <a href="#A3" title="Appendix C Direction Discovery and Steering Ablation Study ‣ Asking Forever: Universal Activations Behind Turn Amplification in Conversational LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">C</span></a>.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S4" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">4 </span>Empirical Evaluation</h2>

<div id="S4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We evaluate whether our direction discovery method (§<a href="#S3.SS2" title="3.2 Discovering Turn-Amplifying Directions ‣ 3 Turn-Amplification in Conversational LLMs ‣ Asking Forever: Universal Activations Behind Turn Amplification in Conversational LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.2</span></a>) can effectively induce turn amplification.
Here, we assume a malicious model integrator that modifies internal activations at runtime; see scenario <span id="S4.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">A1</span> in Appendix <a href="#A2" title="Appendix B Motivating Attack Scenarios ‣ Asking Forever: Universal Activations Behind Turn Amplification in Conversational LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">B</span></a> for more details.
We study additional attack scenarios and vectors in §<a href="#S5" title="5 Practical Attack Instantiations ‣ Asking Forever: Universal Activations Behind Turn Amplification in Conversational LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<section id="S4.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.1 </span>Experimental Setup</h3>

<div id="S4.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Maximum turns.</span>
We set the maximum number of turns in our evaluation to 10 to assess the impact of turn amplification under extended interactions.
We note that the goal of our evaluation is to measure a model’s <em id="S4.SS1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">propensity</em> to prolong interactions, not to predict whether users will respond.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Models.</span>
We evaluate four instruction-tuned LLMs: Qwen2.5-3B <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yang et al., 2025</a>)</cite>, Llama3-8B <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">Grattafiori et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, Falcon3-10B <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">Falcon-LLM Team, 2024</a>)</cite>, and Mistral-22B <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">Mistral AI Team, 2025</a>)</cite>.
These models span distinct families and parameter scales (3–22B), allowing us to assess the generality of our method across architectures.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS1.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS1.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Datasets.</span>
We evaluate turn-amplifying behavior across two benchmarks.
For general-purpose question answering, we sample 250 prompts from Alpaca <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">Taori et al., 2023</a>)</cite>, disjoint from the training prompts (§<a href="#S3.SS2.SSS1" title="3.2.1 Synthetic Data Generation ‣ 3.2 Discovering Turn-Amplifying Directions ‣ 3 Turn-Amplification in Conversational LLMs ‣ Asking Forever: Universal Activations Behind Turn Amplification in Conversational LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.2.1</span></a>).
To assess generation quality and factual correctness, we sample an additional 250 prompts from GSM8K <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">Cobbe et al., 2021</a>)</cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS1.p4" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS1.p4.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS1.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Baselines.</span>
As turn-prolonging behavior has not been systematically studied, there are no established baselines.
We therefore introduce three baseline approaches:
<span id="S4.SS1.p4.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">No Attack</span>: the unmodified model, allowing us to measure baseline turn-prolonging tendencies; <span id="S4.SS1.p4.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Prefilling</span>: at each turn, the assistant response is prefixed with “Can you clarify”, encouraging clarifying questions with minimal intervention;
<span id="S4.SS1.p4.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">System Message</span>: we include a system message (shown in Appendix <a href="#A5.SS3" title="E.3 System-Message Attack Prompt ‣ Appendix E LLM Prompt Specifications ‣ Asking Forever: Universal Activations Behind Turn Amplification in Conversational LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">E.3</span></a>) instructing the model to avoid answering the user query and instead prolong the interaction.
The latter two baselines operate by modifying the model’s inputs or outputs, providing a point of comparison for our method, which instead intervenes directly on internal representations.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.2 </span>Main Results</h3>

<div id="S4.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Evaluation methodology.</span>
For each model, we identify turn-amplifying directions using the procedure in §<a href="#S3.SS2" title="3.2 Discovering Turn-Amplifying Directions ‣ 3 Turn-Amplification in Conversational LLMs ‣ Asking Forever: Universal Activations Behind Turn Amplification in Conversational LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.2</span></a>.
We then evaluate our method and all baselines using our auditing framework (§<a href="#S3.SS1" title="3.1 Our Turn-Amplification Auditing Framework ‣ 3 Turn-Amplification in Conversational LLMs ‣ Asking Forever: Universal Activations Behind Turn Amplification in Conversational LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.1</span></a>) on 500 prompts, aggregating metrics (§<a href="#S3.SS1.SSS3" title="3.1.3 Metrics ‣ 3.1 Our Turn-Amplification Auditing Framework ‣ 3 Turn-Amplification in Conversational LLMs ‣ Asking Forever: Universal Activations Behind Turn Amplification in Conversational LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.1.3</span></a>) over up to 10 turns per conversation.
We compute accuracy for GSM8K but not for Alpaca, which lacks ground-truth labels.
Accuracy is measured over <em id="S4.SS2.p1.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">valid</em> responses only, defined as generations producing a numerical answer in the required <span id="S4.SS2.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">\boxed{}</span> format.
Input and output token counts are computed using each model’s tokenizer.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS2.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Results.</span>
Table <a href="#S3.T1" title="Table 1 ‣ 3.2.2 Turn-Amplifying Direction Optimization ‣ 3.2 Discovering Turn-Amplifying Directions ‣ 3 Turn-Amplification in Conversational LLMs ‣ Asking Forever: Universal Activations Behind Turn Amplification in Conversational LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a> summarizes results across models, datasets, and response modes.
<em id="S4.SS2.p2.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">Our method is the most effective at inducing turn amplification.</em>
On average, it increases the number of turns, input tokens, and output tokens by 8.6<math id="S4.SS2.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>×</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\times</annotation></semantics></math>, 88.2<math id="S4.SS2.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>×</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\times</annotation></semantics></math>, and 4.6<math id="S4.SS2.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>×</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\times</annotation></semantics></math>, respectively, compared to 5.0–5.8<math id="S4.SS2.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>×</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\times</annotation></semantics></math>, 31.9–46.3<math id="S4.SS2.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>×</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\times</annotation></semantics></math>, and 1.3–1.5<math id="S4.SS2.p2.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>×</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\times</annotation></semantics></math> for the baselines.
In the <em id="S4.SS2.p2.1.3" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">worst case</em>, our method induces increases of 9.9<math id="S4.SS2.p2.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>×</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\times</annotation></semantics></math>, 200.1<math id="S4.SS2.p2.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>×</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\times</annotation></semantics></math>, and 6.4<math id="S4.SS2.p2.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>×</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\times</annotation></semantics></math> across these metrics.
Input tokens are particularly affected, as the full conversation history is included as context at each turn, leading to disproportionate amplification.
Assuming output tokens cost 5<math id="S4.SS2.p2.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>×</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\times</annotation></semantics></math> more than input tokens <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib35" title="" class="ltx_ref">Anthropic, </a>)</cite>, <em id="S4.SS2.p2.1.4" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">our method would increase per-conversation usage costs by 9.6<math id="S4.SS2.p2.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>×</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\times</annotation></semantics></math></em> on average, compared to 3.2–3.7<math id="S4.SS2.p2.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>×</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\times</annotation></semantics></math> for the baselines.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS2.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><em id="S4.SS2.p3.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">Our method generalizes across model families, parameter scales, and user behaviors.</em>
We achieve the largest increases in compute-oriented metrics in 42 of the 48 evaluated combinations, indicating consistent effectiveness.
Since larger models incur higher per-token costs <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib35" title="" class="ltx_ref">Anthropic, </a>; <a href="#bib.bib38" title="" class="ltx_ref">Google, </a>; <a href="#bib.bib37" title="" class="ltx_ref">OpenAI, </a>)</cite>, this generalization implies disproportionate cost inflation as model size increases.
Moreover, performance differs only marginally between the <span id="S4.SS2.p3.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">Easy</span> and <span id="S4.SS2.p3.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">Hard</span> user modes, suggesting robustness to user-specific behaviors.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS2.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.p4.1" class="ltx_p">Finally, <em id="S4.SS2.p4.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">our method largely preserves output quality and correctness.</em>
Accuracy changes range from -20.2% to +8.1%, comparable to the baselines (-12.4% to +3.2%).
The largest degradation occurs for Qwen2.5-3B, which drops by 20.2% in <span id="S4.SS2.p4.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">Hard</span> mode; we hypothesize that smaller models are more sensitive to activation-level interventions.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.3 </span>Mechanistic Analysis</h3>

<div id="S4.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We investigate the mechanistic basis of our turn-amplifying feature directions, asking <em id="S4.SS3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">where</em> in the model they operate and <em id="S4.SS3.p1.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">whether</em> they correspond to pre-existing representations.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S4.F3" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2602.17778v1/intervention_layer.svg" id="S4.F3.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/192;" width="476" height="192"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 3: </span><span id="S4.F3.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Impact of intervention layer on our method’s effectiveness</span> for Qwen2.5-3B. We optimize and steer at each layer <em id="S4.F3.6" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">in isolation</em>; the baseline result in Table <a href="#S3.T1" title="Table 1 ‣ 3.2.2 Turn-Amplifying Direction Optimization ‣ 3.2 Discovering Turn-Amplifying Directions ‣ 3 Turn-Amplification in Conversational LLMs ‣ Asking Forever: Universal Activations Behind Turn Amplification in Conversational LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a> steers at <em id="S4.F3.7" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">all</em> layers.</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S4.SS3.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS3.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS3.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Layer localization.</span>
To localize where activation steering is most effective, we learn a single direction and apply steering at each layer <em id="S4.SS3.p2.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">in isolation</em>.
Figure <a href="#S4.F3" title="Figure 3 ‣ 4.3 Mechanistic Analysis ‣ 4 Empirical Evaluation ‣ Asking Forever: Universal Activations Behind Turn Amplification in Conversational LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a> shows results on Alpaca (<span id="S4.SS3.p2.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">Easy</span> mode) for Qwen2.5-3B.
For comparability, we report percent changes relative to the baseline condition in which steering is applied at all layers (results shown in Table <a href="#S3.T1" title="Table 1 ‣ 3.2.2 Turn-Amplifying Direction Optimization ‣ 3.2 Discovering Turn-Amplifying Directions ‣ 3 Turn-Amplification in Conversational LLMs ‣ Asking Forever: Universal Activations Behind Turn Amplification in Conversational LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>).</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS3.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><em id="S4.SS3.p3.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">Directions identified in earlier layers are more effective.</em>
Steering exclusively at layer 0 achieves 85.9–94.5% of the performance observed under full multi-layer steering.
Intermediate layers (5–20) remain impactful but less effective, reaching 58.9–90.2% of baseline performance.
Effectiveness degrades beyond layer 20, falling to 1.5–30.1% at the final layer.
While turn-amplifying behavior could be explicitly encoded in early layers, we find it more plausible that early-layer interventions are effective because they influence a larger fraction of downstream computation.
Prior work supports this interpretation, suggesting that early Transformer layers primarily encode syntax, whereas later layers increasingly represent task-level information <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib34" title="" class="ltx_ref">Rogers et al., 2020</a>)</cite>.
Still, the success of single-layer steering indicates that turn amplification is a low-dimensional representation.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S4.F4" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2602.17778v1/feature_usage.svg" id="S4.F4.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/183;" width="476" height="183"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 4: </span><span id="S4.F4.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Activation of our features without steering</span> for Llama3-8B at layer 10.
Maximum cosine similarity between learned features and assistant token activations, collected from turn-prolonged inputs.
Horizontal lines show the similarity in default (single-turn) conversations.
Random baseline: 10 uniformly sampled directions.</figcaption>
</figure>

<span id="S4.T2.8.1.1.1.5" class="ltx_tr">
