</figure>
<div id="S4.SS3.p4" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS3.p4.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS3.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Do our learned directions corresponding to <em id="S4.SS3.p4.1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">pre-existing</em> internal representations?</span>
We test whether models activate our turn-amplifying directions even without intervention by measuring their <em id="S4.SS3.p4.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">similarity</em> to natural activations.
We collect activations under two conditions: (1) default conversations, and (2) conversations generated using our method.
For each layer and example, we compute the maximum cosine similarity between the learned feature vector and all assistant-token activations, then average across examples.
We take the maximum over tokens because turn-prolonging behavior may manifest at different points in a response.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS3.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.p5.1" class="ltx_p">Figure <a href="#S4.F4" title="Figure 4 ‣ 4.3 Mechanistic Analysis ‣ 4 Empirical Evaluation ‣ Asking Forever: Universal Activations Behind Turn Amplification in Conversational LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a> reports results for Llama3-8B at layer 10, which exhibits the strongest separation between steered and default conditions (see Appendix <a href="#A4" title="Appendix D Layer-Wise Analysis of Turn-Amplifying Features ‣ Asking Forever: Universal Activations Behind Turn Amplification in Conversational LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">D</span></a> for all layers).
Horizontal lines indicate the baseline similarity observed in default single-turn conversations.
For comparison, we also show cosine similarities with 10 randomly sampled directions.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS3.p6" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.p6.1" class="ltx_p"><em id="S4.SS3.p6.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">Models naturally generate activations aligned with our turn-amplifying directions.</em>
During turn-prolonged interactions, maximum cosine similarity increases by 8–51% relative to default conversations, indicating that models possess aligned internal structure even without steering.
Alignment is also substantially higher than with random directions, suggesting that they capture meaningful representations.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S5" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">5 </span>Practical Attack Instantiations</h2>

<div id="S5.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We further investigate whether adversaries can achieve turn-amplification via practical attack vectors.
Specifically, we ask: <em id="S5.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">can the representational structure exploited by our activation steering-based attack also be abused through one-time parameter-level modifications</em>?
See Appendix <a href="#A2" title="Appendix B Motivating Attack Scenarios ‣ Asking Forever: Universal Activations Behind Turn Amplification in Conversational LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">B</span></a> for motivating scenarios (<span id="S5.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">A2</span>, <span id="S5.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">A3</span>) of each attack vector.</p>
</div>
<section id="S5.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">5.1 </span>Supply Chain Attacks via Fine-Tuning</h3>

<div id="S5.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The effectiveness of activation steering suggests that turn-amplifying behavior can be embedded as low-rank structure in weight space via <em id="S5.SS1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">LoRA fine-tuning</em> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib40" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hu et al., 2022</a>)</cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S5.SS1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Threat model.</span>
We instantiate attack scenario <span id="S5.SS1.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">A2</span>: a supply-chain adversary who uses LoRA fine-tuning to implant turn-amplifying behavior into an LLM that is later distributed via public platforms (e.g., HuggingFace <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib41" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wolf et al., 2020</a>)</cite> or TensorFlow Hub <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib42" title="" class="ltx_ref">TensorFlow, </a>)</cite>).
The attacker may release either a fully merged model or standalone LoRA adapters, both common deployment practices <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib45" title="" class="ltx_ref">HuggingFace, </a>; <a href="#bib.bib46" title="" class="ltx_ref">HuggingFace, </a>)</cite>.
Unsuspecting users who deploy these models incur substantially increased inference-time costs.
We assume white-box access to the target model, consistent with prior work on model backdooring <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib43" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hong et al., 2022</a>; <a href="#bib.bib44" title="" class="ltx_ref">Gu et al., 2017</a>)</cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS1.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S5.SS1.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Attack mechanism.</span>
The attacker fine-tunes the model to minimize the turn-amplifying objective <math id="S5.SS1.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{TA}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mi>TA</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{TA}}</annotation></semantics></math> (Eq. <a href="#S3.E2" title="Equation 2 ‣ 3.2.2 Turn-Amplifying Direction Optimization ‣ 3.2 Discovering Turn-Amplifying Directions ‣ 3 Turn-Amplification in Conversational LLMs ‣ Asking Forever: Universal Activations Behind Turn Amplification in Conversational LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>) <em id="S5.SS1.p3.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">without additive activation interventions</em>.
Following <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib40" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hu et al. (2022)</a></cite>, we apply low-rank updates to each linear layer:</p>
<table id="S5.Ex1" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S5.Ex1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="W\leftarrow W+BA,\quad W\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times k},\;B\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times r},\;A\in\mathbb{R}^{r\times k}." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><mi>W</mi><mo stretchy="false">←</mo><mrow><mi>W</mi><mo>+</mo><mrow><mi>B</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>A</mi></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="1.167em">,</mo><mrow><mi>W</mi><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow></msup></mrow><mo rspace="0.447em">,</mo><mrow><mi>B</mi><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi>r</mi></mrow></msup></mrow><mo rspace="0.447em">,</mo><mrow><mi>A</mi><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow></msup></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">W\leftarrow W+BA,\quad W\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times k},\;B\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times r},\;A\in\mathbb{R}^{r\times k}.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S5.SS1.p3.2" class="ltx_p">We evaluate two ranks.
First, <math id="S5.SS1.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="r=1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r=1</annotation></semantics></math> tests whether turn amplification can be induced via a single-rank update, analogous to linear activation steering.
Second, <math id="S5.SS1.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="r=16" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>16</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r=16</annotation></semantics></math> assesses the effect of higher-rank adaptations.
We train on <math id="S5.SS1.p3.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="N=5{,}000" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>5,000</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">N=5{,}000</annotation></semantics></math> samples, matching §<a href="#S3.SS2" title="3.2 Discovering Turn-Amplifying Directions ‣ 3 Turn-Amplification in Conversational LLMs ‣ Asking Forever: Universal Activations Behind Turn Amplification in Conversational LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.2</span></a>; full details are in Appendix <a href="#A1.SS3" title="A.3 LoRA Fine-Tuning Details ‣ Appendix A Detailed Experimental Setup ‣ Asking Forever: Universal Activations Behind Turn Amplification in Conversational LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">A.3</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS1.p4" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS1.p4.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S5.SS1.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Results.</span>
We train rank-1 and rank-16 LoRA adapters on Qwen2.5-3B and Llama3-8B, merge them into the base models, and evaluate on Alpaca and GSM8K (<span id="S5.SS1.p4.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">Easy</span> mode) using the protocol in §<a href="#S4" title="4 Empirical Evaluation ‣ Asking Forever: Universal Activations Behind Turn Amplification in Conversational LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>.
Results are shown in Table <a href="#S4.T2" title="Table 2 ‣ 4.3 Mechanistic Analysis ‣ 4 Empirical Evaluation ‣ Asking Forever: Universal Activations Behind Turn Amplification in Conversational LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>.
Because LoRA induces unconditional turn amplification, <math id="S5.SS1.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\leq" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>≤</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\leq</annotation></semantics></math>4 GSM8K responses are valid in all cases, preventing reliable accuracy computation (we omit such cases).</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS1.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS1.p5.1" class="ltx_p"><em id="S5.SS1.p5.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">LoRA fine-tuning successfully implants turn-amplifying behavior.</em>
By training just <math id="S5.SS1.p5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="3.3\times 10^{-2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>3.3</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><msup><mn>10</mn><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">3.3\times 10^{-2}</annotation></semantics></math>% to <math id="S5.SS1.p5.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="9.6\times 10^{-1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>9.6</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><msup><mn>10</mn><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">9.6\times 10^{-1}</annotation></semantics></math>% of model parameters, we observe 6.6–9.2<math id="S5.SS1.p5.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>×</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\times</annotation></semantics></math> increases in turns, 11.7–116.5<math id="S5.SS1.p5.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>×</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\times</annotation></semantics></math> in input tokens, and 2.0–6.0<math id="S5.SS1.p5.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>×</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\times</annotation></semantics></math> in output tokens, comparable to activation steering and translating to a 3.8–15.2<math id="S5.SS1.p5.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>×</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\times</annotation></semantics></math> increase in usage costs under typical API pricing <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib35" title="" class="ltx_ref">Anthropic, </a>)</cite>.
Increasing <math id="S5.SS1.p5.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="r" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>r</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r</annotation></semantics></math> from 1 to 16 yields only marginal gains (1.5–14.4%), suggesting that turn amplification is encoded in a low-rank subspace of the weight space.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S5.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">5.2 </span>Runtime Attacks via Bit-Flip Corruption</h3>

<div id="S5.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We next evaluate whether turn-amplification can be achieved via extremely localized, bit-level weight corruption.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S5.SS2.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Threat model.</span>
We instantiate attack scenario <span id="S5.SS2.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">A3</span>, assuming an infrastructure adversary capable of inducing targeted bit flips on GPUs (e.g., NVIDIA A6000) via Rowhammer <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib25" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kim et al., 2014</a>)</cite>.
The victim runs an LLM in a resource-sharing environment (e.g., multi-tenant cloud settings) where such attacks have been shown to be feasible <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib33" title="" class="ltx_ref">Coalson et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib26" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lin et al., 2025</a>)</cite>.
The attacker aims to induce a turn-amplifying state <em id="S5.SS2.p2.1.3" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">at runtime</em>, increasing deployment costs until the model is reloaded.
Aligned with prior work <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib55" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yao et al., 2020</a>; <a href="#bib.bib56" title="" class="ltx_ref">Rakin et al., 2019</a>; <a href="#bib.bib33" title="" class="ltx_ref">Coalson et al., 2025</a>)</cite>, we assume white-box access to model parameters.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS2.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS2.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S5.SS2.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Identifying target bits.</span>
Following prior work <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib56" title="" class="ltx_ref">Rakin et al., 2019</a>)</cite>, we conduct an iterative, gradient-guided bit-search.
At each iteration, each weight <math id="S5.SS2.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="w" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>w</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">w</annotation></semantics></math> is assigned a score
<math id="S5.SS2.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{I}_{w}=|\nabla_{w}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{TA}}|" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℐ</mi><mi>w</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mrow><msub><mo rspace="0.167em">∇</mo><mi>w</mi></msub><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mi>TA</mi></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{I}_{w}=|\nabla_{w}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{TA}}|</annotation></semantics></math>,
computed over a set of <math id="S5.SS2.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="N=64" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>64</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">N=64</annotation></semantics></math> conversations; <em id="S5.SS2.p3.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">steering is not applied</em>.
For each layer, we select the top-<math id="S5.SS2.p3.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math> weights (<math id="S5.SS2.p3.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k=10" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>10</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k=10</annotation></semantics></math>) and test flips to the five most significant bits, recording changes in <math id="S5.SS2.p3.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{TA}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mi>TA</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{TA}}</annotation></semantics></math>.
Finally, we apply the bit flip that yields the greatest loss reduction.
This process repeats until reaching <math id="S5.SS2.p3.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="b_{\mathrm{max}}=25" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>b</mi><mi>max</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>25</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">b_{\mathrm{max}}=25</annotation></semantics></math>, a limit shown to be feasible under real-world fault-injection constraints <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib33" title="" class="ltx_ref">Coalson et al., 2025</a>)</cite>.
See Appendix <a href="#A1.SS4" title="A.4 Bit-Flip Attack Details ‣ Appendix A Detailed Experimental Setup ‣ Asking Forever: Universal Activations Behind Turn Amplification in Conversational LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">A.4</span></a> for the detailed algorithm.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS2.p4" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS2.p4.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S5.SS2.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Attack mechanism.</span>
After identifying target bits, the attacker first locates vulnerable bit positions in GPU memory.
Next, the attacker manipulates the system’s memory allocator to place the victim’s LLM in GPU regions that overlap with these vulnerable locations.
Finally, the attacker induces bit-flips at the targeted positions via Rowhammer, resulting in persistent corruption of the model until it is reloaded.
We refer readers to prior work <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib26" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lin et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib33" title="" class="ltx_ref">Coalson et al., 2025</a>)</cite> for a detailed description of the exploitation process.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS2.p5" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS2.p5.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S5.SS2.p5.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Results.</span>
We apply 25 targeted bit flips to Qwen2.5-3B and Llama3-8B; results are shown in Table <a href="#S4.T2" title="Table 2 ‣ 4.3 Mechanistic Analysis ‣ 4 Empirical Evaluation ‣ Asking Forever: Universal Activations Behind Turn Amplification in Conversational LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>.
Despite modifying just <em id="S5.SS2.p5.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">25 weights</em> (3.1–8.3<math id="S5.SS2.p5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\times 10^{-7}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><msup><mn>10</mn><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>7</mn></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\times 10^{-7}</annotation></semantics></math>% of parameters), <em id="S5.SS2.p5.1.3" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">targeted bit-flips induce measurable turn amplification</em>.
On Alpaca, turns increase by 3.4<math id="S5.SS2.p5.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>×</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\times</annotation></semantics></math>, input tokens by 18.6<math id="S5.SS2.p5.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>×</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\times</annotation></semantics></math>, and output tokens by 1.6<math id="S5.SS2.p5.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>×</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\times</annotation></semantics></math>—<math id="S5.SS2.p5.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sim" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>∼</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sim</annotation></semantics></math>25–50% of the results achieved via fine-tuning.
This suggests a sparse, weight-level representation.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS2.p6" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS2.p6.1" class="ltx_p">On GSM8K, effects are weaker (1.3–13.2<math id="S5.SS2.p6.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>×</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\times</annotation></semantics></math>), which we attribute to the use of general QA data (from Alpaca) during bit-search; given the small number of modified parameters, the induced behavior may not generalize well.
Nevertheless, accuracy remains largely intact (changes of <math id="S5.SS2.p6.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="-11.5\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><mn>11.5</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">-11.5\%</annotation></semantics></math> to <math id="S5.SS2.p6.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="-5.4\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><mn>5.4</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">-5.4\%</annotation></semantics></math>), indicating minimal degradation of output quality.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S6" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">6 </span>Discussion: Potential Countermeasures</h2>

<div id="S6.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Prior work has proposed several defenses against cost-amplification, including <em id="S6.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">input filtering</em> based on content or perplexity <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib57" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhu et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib58" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhang et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib59" title="" class="ltx_ref">Li et al., 2025a</a>; <a href="#bib.bib30" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kumar et al., 2025</a>)</cite>, <em id="S6.p1.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">early stopping</em> when outputs stabilize <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib59" title="" class="ltx_ref">Li et al., 2025a</a>)</cite>, <em id="S6.p1.1.3" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">guardrail models</em> for detecting erroneous content <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib58" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhang et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib57" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhu et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib27" title="" class="ltx_ref">Feng et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, and <em id="S6.p1.1.4" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">pattern-based detectors</em> that flag suspicious outputs <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib57" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhu et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib60" title="" class="ltx_ref">Li et al., 2025b</a>)</cite>.
However, these defenses target anomalous single-turn inputs and do not address attacks operating over many benign turns.</p>
</div>
<div id="S6.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.p2.1" class="ltx_p">We explore preliminary countermeasures tailored to turn-amplification.
To ensure applicability across all attack vectors, we focus on generalizable, prompt-based techniques that require no model modification or internal access:
<span id="S6.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Defensive System Message</span>: we investigate whether a system prompt (shown in Appendix <a href="#A5.SS4" title="E.4 System-Message Defense Prompt ‣ Appendix E LLM Prompt Specifications ‣ Asking Forever: Universal Activations Behind Turn Amplification in Conversational LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">E.4</span></a>) can mitigate turn amplification by instructing models to provide complete, direct answers to all queries and to ask clarifying questions only when necessary;
<span id="S6.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Few-Shot Prompting</span>: we collect 5 direct answers to Alpaca queries from Llama3-8B and prepend them to all subsequent conversations to encourage concise, direct answers via in-context learning <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib61" title="" class="ltx_ref">Brown et al., 2020</a>)</cite>.</p>
</div>

<div id="S6.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S6.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S6.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Results.</span>
Table <a href="#S6.T3" title="Table 3 ‣ 6 Discussion: Potential Countermeasures ‣ Asking Forever: Universal Activations Behind Turn Amplification in Conversational LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a> reports results for Llama3-8B on Alpaca (<span id="S6.p3.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">Easy</span> mode).
Overall, the evaluated defenses are largely ineffective.
The defensive system prompt has minimal impact in most settings, with its only substantial effect against the bit-flip attack (reductions of 37–57%).
Notably, our activation steering and LoRA fine-tuning methods remain robust to explicit instructions for directly answering queries.</p>
</div>
<div id="S6.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.p4.1" class="ltx_p">Few-shot prompting is more effective, reducing turns by 78.8% for the System Message baseline, 23.5% for steering, and 16.7% for LoRA.
This suggests that in-context learning exerts stronger control over generation than system-level instructions.
However, it incurs substantial overhead: even for benign queries, it increases input tokens by 58<math id="S6.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>×</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\times</annotation></semantics></math> and output tokens by 2.7<math id="S6.p4.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>×</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\times</annotation></semantics></math>.
Although prompt caching <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib36" title="" class="ltx_ref">Anthropic, </a>)</cite> may amortize some costs in practice, the overhead remains prohibitive.
Our findings indicate that future work is necessary to design effective turn-amplification mitigation strategies.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S7" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">7 </span>Conclusion</h2>

<div id="S7.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S7.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We introduce <em id="S7.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">turn amplification</em>: a previously unexplored cost-amplification attack that prolongs multi-turn interactions.
To study this unique failure mode, we develop an interaction-level auditing framework and identify <em id="S7.p1.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">universal</em> activation directions in LLMs that underlie turn-amplifying behaviors.
We demonstrate three attack vectors—activation steering, LoRA fine-tuning, and targeted bit-flips—and observe up to 9.9<math id="S7.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>×</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\times</annotation></semantics></math> longer conversations, with up to 200.1<math id="S7.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>×</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\times</annotation></semantics></math> and 6.4<math id="S7.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>×</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\times</annotation></semantics></math> more input and output tokens across four LLMs and two benchmarks.
We evaluate preliminary defenses and find them ineffective, underscoring the need to treat conversational dynamics as a first-class security concern.</p>
</div>
<div class="ltx_pagination ltx_role_newpage"></div>
</section>
<section id="Sx1" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section">Impact Statement</h2>

<div id="Sx1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Our work characterizes a previously underexplored class of risks in deployed conversational LLMs: interaction-level cost amplification through persistent multi-turn dynamics. By identifying and analyzing turn amplification, our methods and findings help practitioners, system designers, and model providers better understand, assess, and mitigate inefficiencies in real-world conversational systems. More broadly, this work encourages research on attestation and countermeasures that move beyond single-turn attacks to account for long-horizon interaction behavior.</p>
</div>
<div id="Sx1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Note that our work does <em id="Sx1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">not</em> open up new attack capabilities. Rather, it systematizes a failure mode that can already arise from common conversational behaviors such as clarification-seeking. Our demonstrations are limited to open-source models and controlled research settings, and are intended to illustrate the existence and severity of interaction-level cost amplification, rather than to provide turnkey mechanisms for exploiting deployed conversational systems.</p>
</div>
<div id="Sx1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Identifying this failure mode is important for improving the robustness, transparency, and cost efficiency of conversational AI systems. By characterizing turn amplification as a mechanistically grounded risk, our work motivates future research on detecting, auditing, and mitigating interaction-level vulnerabilities in AI deployments at scale.</p>
</div>
</section>

<section id="A1" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix A </span>Detailed Experimental Setup</h2>

<section id="A1.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">A.1 </span>Hardware and Software</h3>

<div id="A1.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We implement our method using Python v3.10.19 and PyTorch v2.5.1 with CUDA 12.4.
All language models and datasets used in our work are open-source and available on HuggingFace <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib41" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wolf et al., 2020</a>)</cite> or their respective repositories.
We run all experiments on two machines: the first has an Intel Xeon Processor with 48 cores, 768GB of memory, and 8 Nvidia A40 GPUs.
The second has an Intel Xeon Processor with 112 cores, 2TB of memory, and 8 Nvidia H100 GPUs.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A1.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">A.2 </span>Direction Optimization Details</h3>

<div id="A1.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A1.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.SS2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Hyperparameters and setup.</span>
Across all models, we optimize directions for <math id="A1.SS2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="K=10" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>K</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>10</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">K=10</annotation></semantics></math> training iterations using a learning rate of <math id="A1.SS2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\eta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>η</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\eta</annotation></semantics></math> = 1e-2. Directions are randomly initialized from a Gaussian distribution with mean <math id="A1.SS2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mu=0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>μ</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mu=0</annotation></semantics></math> and standard deviation <math id="A1.SS2.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sigma=0.05" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>σ</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0.05</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sigma=0.05</annotation></semantics></math>.
As described in §<a href="#S3.SS2.SSS2" title="3.2.2 Turn-Amplifying Direction Optimization ‣ 3.2 Discovering Turn-Amplifying Directions ‣ 3 Turn-Amplification in Conversational LLMs ‣ Asking Forever: Universal Activations Behind Turn Amplification in Conversational LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.2.2</span></a>, training is performed on <math id="A1.SS2.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{S}=5{,}000" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒮</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>5,000</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{S}=5{,}000</annotation></semantics></math> uniformly sampled conversation–turn pairs from <math id="A1.SS2.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{train}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒟</mi><mi>train</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{train}}</annotation></semantics></math>, and directions are learned across all layers (i.e., Transformer block outputs).
We use an effective batch size of 16 via gradient accumulation, with the per-sample batch size set to the maximum value that avoids out-of-memory errors.
To improve training stability, we apply gradient clipping with a threshold of 10.</p>
</div>
<div id="A1.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A1.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.SS2.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Training procedure.</span>
In addition to the procedure outlined in Algorithm <a href="#alg1" title="Algorithm 1 ‣ 3.2.2 Turn-Amplifying Direction Optimization ‣ 3.2 Discovering Turn-Amplifying Directions ‣ 3 Turn-Amplification in Conversational LLMs ‣ Asking Forever: Universal Activations Behind Turn Amplification in Conversational LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>, we employ a validation-based early-stopping criterion to determine when to terminate training.
Specifically, we sample a hold-out validation set of 500 conversation–turn pairs and evaluate the validation loss 10 times per epoch.
If the validation loss fails to improve for three consecutive evaluations, we stop training and return the final directions.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A1.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">A.3 </span>LoRA Fine-Tuning Details</h3>

<div id="A1.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A1.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.SS3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Hyperparameters and setup.</span>
Across all models, we optimize LoRA modules for <math id="A1.SS3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="K=10" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>K</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>10</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">K=10</annotation></semantics></math> training iterations using a learning rate of <math id="A1.SS3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\eta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>η</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\eta</annotation></semantics></math> = 5e-4.
As described in §<a href="#S5.SS1" title="5.1 Supply Chain Attacks via Fine-Tuning ‣ 5 Practical Attack Instantiations ‣ Asking Forever: Universal Activations Behind Turn Amplification in Conversational LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5.1</span></a>, training is performed on <math id="A1.SS3.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{S}=5{,}000" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒮</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>5,000</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{S}=5{,}000</annotation></semantics></math> uniformly sampled conversation–turn pairs from <math id="A1.SS3.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{train}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒟</mi><mi>train</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{train}}</annotation></semantics></math>, and LoRA adapters are fit to all linear weight matrices in the MLP and self-attention layers.
Each LoRA module uses a scaling factor of <math id="A1.SS3.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\alpha=32" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>α</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>32</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\alpha=32</annotation></semantics></math> and a dropout probability of 0.05 to promote generalization.
We use an effective batch size of 16 via gradient accumulation, with the per-sample batch size set to the maximum value that avoids out-of-memory errors.
To improve training stability, we apply gradient clipping with a threshold of 1.</p>
</div>
<div id="A1.SS3.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A1.SS3.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.SS3.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Training procedure.</span>
As in direction optimization (Appendix <a href="#A1.SS2" title="A.2 Direction Optimization Details ‣ Appendix A Detailed Experimental Setup ‣ Asking Forever: Universal Activations Behind Turn Amplification in Conversational LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">A.2</span></a>), we periodically compute the validation loss and use a patience-based early stopping criterion.
After training, we return the final LoRA modules.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A1.SS4" class="ltx_subsection">

<div id="A1.SS4.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A1.SS4.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.SS4.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Hyperparameters and setup.</span>
As described in §<a href="#S5.SS2" title="5.2 Runtime Attacks via Bit-Flip Corruption ‣ 5 Practical Attack Instantiations ‣ Asking Forever: Universal Activations Behind Turn Amplification in Conversational LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5.2</span></a>, we use <math id="A1.SS4.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="N=64" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>64</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">N=64</annotation></semantics></math> randomly sampled conversation–turn pairs to compute <math id="A1.SS4.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{TA}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mi>TA</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{TA}}</annotation></semantics></math>. We use significantly fewer examples than for our attack vectors, as bit-search on LLMs is highly computationally intensive <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib33" title="" class="ltx_ref">Coalson et al., 2025</a>)</cite>.
Furthermore, due to memory constraints, we sample conversations with a maximum of three turns rather than ten.
To balance feasibility and effectiveness, we analyze the top <math id="A1.SS4.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k=10" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>10</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k=10</annotation></semantics></math> weights per layer according to the importance score <math id="A1.SS4.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{I}_{w}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℐ</mi><mi>w</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{I}_{w}</annotation></semantics></math>.
In all experiments, we perform exactly <math id="A1.SS4.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="b_{\mathrm{max}}=25" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>b</mi><mi>max</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>25</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">b_{\mathrm{max}}=25</annotation></semantics></math> bit flips.
All weights are in <span id="A1.SS4.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">float16</span> format.</p>
</div>
<div id="A1.SS4.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A1.SS4.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.SS4.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Detailed algorithm.</span>
Algorithm <a href="#alg2" title="Algorithm 2 ‣ A.4 Bit-Flip Attack Details ‣ Appendix A Detailed Experimental Setup ‣ Asking Forever: Universal Activations Behind Turn Amplification in Conversational LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a> presents the pseudocode for our gradient-guided bit-search procedure, which iteratively identifies and flips individual weight bits to induce turn amplification.
We first sample a fixed set of <math id="A1.SS4.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="N" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>N</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">N</annotation></semantics></math> conversations. At each iteration, we <span id="A1.SS4.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">(Lines 5–6)</span> compute the turn-amplifying loss <math id="A1.SS4.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{TA}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mi>TA</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{TA}}</annotation></semantics></math> and the corresponding gradient magnitudes <math id="A1.SS4.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{I}_{w}=\lvert\nabla_{w}\mathcal{L}\rvert" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℐ</mi><mi>w</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mrow><msub><mo rspace="0.167em">∇</mo><mi>w</mi></msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{I}_{w}=\lvert\nabla_{w}\mathcal{L}\rvert</annotation></semantics></math> for all weights. Note that <math id="A1.SS4.p2.m4" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{TA}}(C,t,\cdot)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mi>TA</mi></msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>C</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi><mo rspace="0em">,</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">⋅</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{TA}}(C,t,\cdot)</annotation></semantics></math> uses a placeholder ‘<math id="A1.SS4.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\cdot" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>⋅</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\cdot</annotation></semantics></math>’ to indicate that no steering is applied during this phase.
Next, we <span id="A1.SS4.p2.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">(Lines 8–16)</span> enumerate candidate bit flips by selecting the top-<math id="A1.SS4.p2.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math> weights per layer and evaluating flips to their five most significant bits, recording the resulting loss reduction <math id="A1.SS4.p2.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Delta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Delta</annotation></semantics></math>; here, <math id="A1.SS4.p2.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="L" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>L</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">L</annotation></semantics></math> is <em id="A1.SS4.p2.1.4" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">every</em> weight matrix in the model except the embedding matrices.
Finally, we <span id="A1.SS4.p2.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">(Lines 19–21)</span> greedily apply the single bit flip yielding the largest <math id="A1.SS4.p2.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Delta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Delta</annotation></semantics></math> and add it to the set of flipped bits <math id="A1.SS4.p2.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{B}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℬ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{B}</annotation></semantics></math>.
This procedure repeats until <math id="A1.SS4.p2.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="b_{\mathrm{max}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>b</mi><mi>max</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">b_{\mathrm{max}}</annotation></semantics></math> total bit flips are applied, after which <math id="A1.SS4.p2.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{B}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℬ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{B}</annotation></semantics></math> is returned.
Our approach closely follows standard gradient-guided bit-search methods in the literature <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib55" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yao et al., 2020</a>; <a href="#bib.bib56" title="" class="ltx_ref">Rakin et al., 2019</a>; <a href="#bib.bib33" title="" class="ltx_ref">Coalson et al., 2025</a>)</cite>.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="A2" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix B </span>Motivating Attack Scenarios</h2>

<div id="A2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To our knowledge, this is the first work to study adversaries
that increase the operational cost of deployed conversational LLMs
by inducing prolonged multi-turn interactions.
Unlike prior cost-amplification attacks that rely on carefully crafted prompts at inference time, this attacker exploits stable conversational dynamics that persist across prompts, tasks, and users.
Because the attack operates at the behavioral level, the adversary does not require repeated prompt-level optimization at inference time,
making turn amplification a scalable and practical threat.</p>
</div>
<div id="A2.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A2.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A2.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Attack scenarios.</span>
Turn amplification can be exploited by adversaries
operating at different points in the conversational LLM ecosystem.
We categorize them into three classes
based on adversary access and deployment context.</p>
<ul id="A2.I1" class="ltx_itemize" style="--ltx-enum-leftmargin:1.8em;">
<li id="A2.I1.ix1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item"><span id="A2.I1.ix1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">A1.</span></span> 
<div id="A2.I1.ix1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.I1.ix1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A2.I1.ix1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Malicious integrators</span> (§<a href="#S4" title="4 Empirical Evaluation ‣ Asking Forever: Universal Activations Behind Turn Amplification in Conversational LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>).
In deployment pipelines where third parties provide inference infrastructure or API wrappers, an adversary with white-box runtime access can apply activation-level interventions to bias model behavior.
Such integrators can inject steering vectors to induce persistent turn amplification without modifying the underlying model weights.
Motivations include inflating usage statistics for billing fraud,
trapping agentic LLMs in clarification loops to waste compute,
or degrading user experience to harm a competitor’s service.
While this threat model requires runtime access to model internals, it represents a realistic concern in complex ML supply chains where model owners do not control the full serving stack.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="A2.I1.ix2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item"><span id="A2.I1.ix2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">A2.</span></span> 
<div id="A2.I1.ix2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.I1.ix2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A2.I1.ix2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Supply-chain adversaries</span> (§<a href="#S5.SS1" title="5.1 Supply Chain Attacks via Fine-Tuning ‣ 5 Practical Attack Instantiations ‣ Asking Forever: Universal Activations Behind Turn Amplification in Conversational LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5.1</span></a>)
can distribute fine-tuned checkpoints or adapters that encode a bias toward clarification-seeking behavior.
Once deployed, such models induce persistent turn amplification
across users and tasks, increasing interaction length and
backend resource consumption for downstream service operators.
This allows adversaries to externalize operational costs
onto victims while remaining difficult to detect due to benign model outputs.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="A2.I1.ix3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item"><span id="A2.I1.ix3.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">A3.</span></span> 
<div id="A2.I1.ix3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.I1.ix3.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A2.I1.ix3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Infrastructure and hosting adversaries</span> (§<a href="#S5.SS2" title="5.2 Runtime Attacks via Bit-Flip Corruption ‣ 5 Practical Attack Instantiations ‣ Asking Forever: Universal Activations Behind Turn Amplification in Conversational LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5.2</span></a>).
In shared or cloud-based model hosting environments,
adversaries can leverage low-level, bit-wise parameter corruptions (via software-level threats like Rowhammer <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib25" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kim et al., 2014</a>)</cite>)
to bias conversational behavior.
Although they may not directly interact with the model
through prompts, their influence at the infrastructure level
can induce persistent turn amplification across all subsequent interactions.</p>
</div></li>
</ul>
</div>
<div id="A2.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A2.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A2.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Adversary capabilities and assumptions.</span>
All three scenarios assume white-box access to model parameters or activations,
but differ in <em id="A2.p3.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">when</em> and <em id="A2.p3.1.3" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">how</em> the adversary intervenes.
<span id="A2.p3.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">A1</span> requires persistent runtime access to inject activation steering at each turn; <span id="A2.p3.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">A2</span> and <span id="A2.p3.1.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">A3</span> require only one-time access to modify weights (via fine-tuning or bit-flips, respectively), after which turn amplification occurs automatically without further involvement.
Crucially, none of our attacks require control over user prompts at inference time, distinguishing turn amplification from prior prompt-level attacks.
We assume the adversary’s goal is to maximize turn count (and thus inference cost) while preserving output quality to avoid detection.
Individual responses should remain fluent, policy-compliant, and superficially helpful.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A3" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix C </span>Direction Discovery and Steering Ablation Study</h2>

<figure id="A3.F5" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2602.17778v1/ablation.svg" id="A3.F5.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/90;" width="476" height="90"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 5: </span><span id="A3.F5.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Impact of key training and intervention configurations on turn-amplification effectiveness</span> for Qwen2.5-3B on Alpaca (<span id="A3.F5.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">Easy</span> mode).
For each metric, we report the percentage change relative to the baseline steering results in Table <a href="#S3.T1" title="Table 1 ‣ 3.2.2 Turn-Amplifying Direction Optimization ‣ 3.2 Discovering Turn-Amplifying Directions ‣ 3 Turn-Amplification in Conversational LLMs ‣ Asking Forever: Universal Activations Behind Turn Amplification in Conversational LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>.</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="A3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A3.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Number of training samples (<math id="A3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="N" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>N</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">N</annotation></semantics></math>)</span>.
We vary the number of samples used for feature optimization (<math id="A3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="N" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>N</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">N</annotation></semantics></math>) in <math id="A3.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\{10,100,1000,5000,10000\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><mn>10,100</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1000</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>5000</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>10000</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\{10,100,1000,5000,10000\}</annotation></semantics></math>.
The leftmost plot in Figure <a href="#A3.F5" title="Figure 5 ‣ Appendix C Direction Discovery and Steering Ablation Study ‣ Asking Forever: Universal Activations Behind Turn Amplification in Conversational LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a> shows the results.
Using <math id="A3.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="N=10" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>10</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">N=10</annotation></semantics></math> is insufficient for finding turn-amplifying features, achieving only 1.3–29.0% of baseline performance; this suggests that such a small sample size hinders generalization.
Performance increases substantially for <math id="A3.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="100\leq N\leq 1000" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>100</mn><mo>≤</mo><mi>N</mi><mo>≤</mo><mn>1000</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">100\leq N\leq 1000</annotation></semantics></math>, reaching 76.4–99.7% of baseline, indicating that relatively few samples are sufficient to uncover universal features.
We observe the best performance at <math id="A3.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="N=5000" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>5000</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">N=5000</annotation></semantics></math>, after which it saturates; we therefore use <math id="A3.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="N=5000" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>5000</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">N=5000</annotation></semantics></math> to balance performance with optimization time.</p>
</div>
<div id="A3.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A3.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A3.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Maximum number of steering turns.</span>
To assess the <em id="A3.p2.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">precision</em> of activation steering, we vary the maximum number of steering turns (<math id="A3.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="T_{\mathrm{max}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>T</mi><mi>max</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">T_{\mathrm{max}}</annotation></semantics></math>) over <math id="A3.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\{1,\dots,9\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><mn>9</mn><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\{1,\dots,9\}</annotation></semantics></math>; results are shown in the middle plot of Figure <a href="#A3.F5" title="Figure 5 ‣ Appendix C Direction Discovery and Steering Ablation Study ‣ Asking Forever: Universal Activations Behind Turn Amplification in Conversational LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a>.
As <math id="A3.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="T_{\mathrm{max}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>T</mi><mi>max</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">T_{\mathrm{max}}</annotation></semantics></math> increases from 1 to 6, the number of assistant turns, input tokens, and output tokens grows linearly, indicating that steering precisely moderates turn amplification behavior across different dialogue positions.
For <math id="A3.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="T_{\mathrm{max}}\geq 7" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>T</mi><mi>max</mi></msub><mo>≥</mo><mn>7</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">T_{\mathrm{max}}\geq 7</annotation></semantics></math>, gains in turn amplification performance begin to saturate; this suggests that additional steering beyond this point provides diminishing returns.</p>
</div>
<div id="A3.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A3.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A3.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Model used for synthetic data generation.</span>
To assess the impact of the size (and thus capabilities) of the model used for synthetic data generation in §<a href="#S3.SS2.SSS1" title="3.2.1 Synthetic Data Generation ‣ 3.2 Discovering Turn-Amplifying Directions ‣ 3 Turn-Amplification in Conversational LLMs ‣ Asking Forever: Universal Activations Behind Turn Amplification in Conversational LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.2.1</span></a>, we evaluate the 1.5B, 7B, 14B, and 32B Qwen2.5 models, with the resulting steering performance shown in the rightmost plot of Figure <a href="#A3.F5" title="Figure 5 ‣ Appendix C Direction Discovery and Steering Ablation Study ‣ Asking Forever: Universal Activations Behind Turn Amplification in Conversational LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a>.
Performance varies substantially across model sizes.
Qwen2.5-1.5B exceeds the baseline performance (which uses Qwen2.5-32B) in terms of turns, but produces significantly fewer input and generated tokens.
The 7B and 14B models similarly struggle, with the 14B model in particular achieving only 34.4–53.0% of baseline performance despite its larger parameter count.
One possible explanation is that reliable instruction following—an essential capability for our data generation pipeline—has been shown to exhibit emergent, non-monotonic scaling behavior, where smaller models often fail to consistently execute instructions despite fluent language modeling <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib39" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wei et al., 2022</a>)</cite>.
We therefore use Qwen2.5-32B, the largest model feasible for our academic study, which empirically yields substantially higher-quality synthetic data than its smaller counterparts.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A4" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix D </span>Layer-Wise Analysis of Turn-Amplifying Features</h2>

<div id="A4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Here, we replicate our feature activation analysis in §<a href="#S4.SS3" title="4.3 Mechanistic Analysis ‣ 4 Empirical Evaluation ‣ Asking Forever: Universal Activations Behind Turn Amplification in Conversational LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4.3</span></a> across all layers of Llama3-8B.
Figure <a href="#A4.F6" title="Figure 6 ‣ Appendix D Layer-Wise Analysis of Turn-Amplifying Features ‣ Asking Forever: Universal Activations Behind Turn Amplification in Conversational LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a> presents the results.</p>
</div>
<div id="A4.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A4.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><em id="A4.p2.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">Feature activation varies significantly across layers.</em>
Early (<math id="A4.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sim" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>∼</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sim</annotation></semantics></math>0–6) and late (<math id="A4.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sim" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>∼</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sim</annotation></semantics></math>14–31) layers appear to leverage our learned activations only minimally on turn-amplifying inputs, suggesting that the features learned at these layers may not be “natively” represented there.
However, we identify a <em id="A4.p2.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">non-trivial</em> subset of middle layers (<math id="A4.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sim" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>∼</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sim</annotation></semantics></math>7–13) that exhibit significantly increased activation in response to turn-amplifying inputs (up to <math id="A4.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sim" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>∼</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sim</annotation></semantics></math>50%), indicating alignment with the model’s natural representations in turn-amplifying contexts.
In all cases, our features are entirely distinct from randomly sampled directions, further supporting the conclusion that they are not noise.</p>
</div>
<div id="A4.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A4.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Note that our analysis is constrained by the complexity of how turn-amplifying behavior is likely represented: the relevant computations may occur at layers other than those where we apply steering, or may involve nonlinear interactions that our analysis does not fully capture.
Moreover, because we learn distinct features at each layer, some features may play roles correlated with turn amplification without being causal, such as maintaining high-fidelity output quality.
Accordingly, our analysis establishes the <em id="A4.p3.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">existence</em> of pre-existing representational structures aligned with turn-amplifying behavior, but we do not claim that these structures are sufficient or fully interpretable.
We leave deeper mechanistic investigation to future work.</p>
</div>

<section id="A5" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix E </span>LLM Prompt Specifications</h2>

<div id="A5.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Here, we present the detailed prompts used in our turn-amplification auditing framework, as well as those used for system-message attacks and defenses.
In all relevant cases, {{<span id="A5.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">conversation</span>}} refers to a string containing the full conversation history between a user and an assistant, properly delimited into turns.</p>
</div>

<section id="A6" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix F </span>Example Conversations</h2>

<div id="A6.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A6.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Here, we present representative conversations from our main empirical evaluation (§<a href="#S4" title="4 Empirical Evaluation ‣ Asking Forever: Universal Activations Behind Turn Amplification in Conversational LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>).
For each subsection, we select one input prompt for each dataset-response mode pair and show the resulting conversations (<em id="A6.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">verbatim</em>) for our method and the baselines, using a single representative model; to ensure completeness, we use a different model in each subsection.</p>
</div>

      should not be a barrier to accessing research. Thank you for your continued support in championing open access for
      all.</p>
